articles.title: Two texts that keep you safe

body.support:
Every chemical at work comes with **two texts**.

**The label** is for when you pick it up. It is quick to read. Every label in Australia has the same parts:

1. **Signal word.** **DANGER** is more serious. **WARNING** is less serious.
2. **Pictogram.** A black picture in a red diamond. A flame means it catches fire.
3. **Hazard.** What it can do to you.
4. **Precautions.** What you must do. *Wear gloves.*

**The safety data sheet (SDS)** is the full story. It is long. You don't read it all. You find the part you need. Every SDS has **16 sections**, always in the same order. First aid is **section 4**.

Your workplace must have the SDS for each chemical. Ask where it is.

The big rule: **no label? Don't use it.**
body.core:
Every hazardous chemical at work comes with two texts. They're about the same chemical, but they're written for **different moments**.

**The label** is for the moment you pick it up. It has to work in seconds, so it uses a set pattern that's the same on every chemical in Australia:

1. **Signal word.** **DANGER** for more serious hazards, **WARNING** for less serious ones.
2. **Pictograms.** Black pictures in red diamonds. A flame means it catches fire easily. Corrosion (liquid eating into a hand) means it can burn skin and eyes.
3. **Hazard statements.** What it can do to you: *Highly flammable liquid and vapour.*
4. **Precautions.** What you must do: *Wear protective gloves. Keep away from heat and hot surfaces.*

**The safety data sheet (SDS)** is the full story. It's longer and more technical, because it has to cover everything: what's in it, first aid, fires, spills, storage, safety gear and more. Nobody reads an SDS from start to finish. You find the part you need, because every SDS has the **same 16 sections in the same order**. First aid is always section 4. Handling and storage is section 7. Your PPE is section 8.

Workplaces must keep current safety data sheets where workers can get to them. Ask where they are on your first day.

One rule beats them all: **if a chemical is in a bottle with no label, don't use it.** If you **decant** a chemical into another container, that container needs a label too.
body.extend:
Every hazardous chemical in an Australian workplace comes with two texts. They share a subject but have very different purposes and audiences.

**The label** is designed for the point of use: a worker holding the container, often in a hurry. Australia uses the Globally Harmonised System (GHS), so labels follow a fixed pattern that can be read in seconds:

1. **Signal word.** **DANGER** signals more severe hazards; **WARNING**, less severe ones.
2. **Pictograms.** Black symbols in red diamonds that show the type of hazard, readable without words.
3. **Hazard statements.** Standard sentences describing the harm: *Causes severe skin burns and eye damage.*
4. **Precautionary statements.** Imperatives telling the reader what to do: *Wear protective gloves. Keep away from heat, hot surfaces, sparks and open flames.*

**The safety data sheet (SDS)** is a reference text for anyone who needs detail: workers, supervisors, first aiders, firefighters. It must cover a lot, so it uses **16 numbered sections in a fixed order**. A reader can go straight to what they need. First aid is section 4; handling and storage, section 7; personal protection, section 8.

Workplaces must keep current SDSs where workers can reach them. And one simple rule beats everything: never use an unlabelled container. If you **decant** a chemical, the new container must be labelled.

caseStudies.title: The wrong bottle

body.support:
In **February 2022**, a worker was cleaning the kitchen at a café in **Wye River**, Victoria.

The worker went to get the grill cleaner. But they grabbed the wrong bottle. It was **metho**. Metho catches fire very easily. The two bottles looked the same. They were kept **side by side**.

The metho caught fire on the grill. The worker's **arm, neck and hair** caught fire.

WorkSafe Victoria charged the business. The business did not have **up-to-date safety data sheets**. It had not **trained** the worker properly.

The business made a legal promise to fix it. It had to train all its staff about chemicals.
body.core:
On **12 February 2022**, a casual worker was cleaning the kitchen at the **Wye River General Store and Café**, on the Great Ocean Road. A labour-hire agency had sent them there.

The worker went out the back to get the grill cleaner. But the bottle they grabbed was **methylated spirits**, which catches fire very easily. The two were kept **side by side in similar bottles**.

On the hot grill, the methylated spirits caught fire. So did the worker's **arm, neck and hair**. The worker ran to a sink. Only then did a co-worker pick up the bottle and see it wasn't grill cleaner.

WorkSafe Victoria charged the business with **eight offences**. Two of them: not keeping **current safety data sheets**, and not properly **training and supervising** the worker.

The case didn't go to court. Instead, the business made WorkSafe an **enforceable undertaking**: a legal promise to fix things. Part of it was chemical safety training for all its staff.
body.extend:
On **12 February 2022**, a labour-hire worker was cleaning the kitchen at the **Wye River General Store and Café** on Victoria's Great Ocean Road.

The worker went to the back room for the grill cleaner. They picked up a bottle of **methylated spirits** instead: a highly flammable liquid. The two products were stored **side by side in similar bottles**. On the hot grill, the methylated spirits ignited, and the worker's **arm, neck and hair** caught fire. Only after the worker had run to a sink did a co-worker pick up the bottle and realise the mistake.

WorkSafe Victoria charged the business with **eight offences** under Victoria's safety laws. They included failing to keep **current safety data sheets** and failing to properly **train and supervise** the worker.

The case didn't go to court. WorkSafe accepted an **enforceable undertaking** instead: a legally binding promise to improve, including chemical safety training for all staff.

The lesson is uncomfortable. Methylated spirits labels warn people to keep it away from heat and flames. But a label only protects you if it's read, and the workplace's systems decide whether it gets read.

teacher.overview: Students compare two workplace texts about the same chemical: the GHS label (instructional, read in seconds at the point of use) and the safety data sheet (informational reference, 16 fixed sections). They annotate both, decode pictograms, choose the right text for workplace problems, and analyse a real Victorian case where a worker caught fire after grabbing methylated spirits instead of grill cleaner. The final task turns a real label and SDS into a safety card for a new worker.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** the label is for the moment you use it (quick, read in seconds); the SDS is the full reference (detail on first aid, storage, PPE and more). Four label parts: signal word, pictogram, hazard statement, precautions. Same 16 sections so anyone can find information fast on any chemical. No label: don't use it, tell your supervisor.

**Label:** 1 product name (match to the SDS); 2 signal word DANGER (more serious); 3 corrosion pictogram (burns skin and eyes); 4 hazard statement (what it does to you); 5 precautions (gloves, eye protection, don't mix); 6 first aid (rinse eyes, call 13 11 26).

**Pictograms:** flame — fire (flammable); corrosion — burns; skull and crossbones — poison (toxic); exclamation mark — harms health (irritant/harmful); flame over circle — fire (oxidiser); person with star — harms health (serious long-term).

**SDS:** 1 identification (right product, emergency number); 2 hazards; 3 first aid (section 4); 4 handling and storage (section 7); 5 personal protection (section 8); 6 date (is it current?).

**Where would you look?:** splash on arm — label first aid, or SDS section 4; gloves and glasses — SDS section 8 (and label precautions); right SDS — compare product name with SDS section 1; up to date — SDS section 16 date.

**Same chemical, two texts:** label — anyone about to use it, at the moment of use, little detail; SDS — workers, supervisors, first aiders, when they need detail or something goes wrong, lots of detail.

**Case study:** similar bottles stored side by side; no current SDSs; worker not properly trained or supervised; the label warning only works if someone reads it; rules such as store flammables away from cleaners, label everything, train every new worker before they clean.

realityCheck: **No hazardous chemicals in class.** Use empty, rinsed containers or photos of labels. Never ask students to bring chemicals from work or home; the final task uses labels and SDSs found online.

**The case is confronting.** A worker catching fire is vivid. The sources don't report how badly the worker was hurt, so don't guess. Keep the focus on the system: similar bottles, no current SDSs, no training.

**Students with jobs are your experts.** Many already use chemicals in fast food, cleaning, salons or on farms. Ask if they've ever been shown the SDS at work. Many haven't, and that's a real conversation about their rights.
**Real SDSs are long and technical.** That's the point of the lesson: model skimming by section number, and let Foundation readers find just sections 2, 4 and 8.
**Works in a real class:** yes, especially for students heading into hospitality, trades, cleaning, hair and beauty or agriculture. It also links well to VET units with a WHS component.
